data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Preferring the better-corroborated theory is defensible on Popper's own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more likely true, but as a critical preference for the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby offering the best available basis for action while remaining open to future refutation; this avoids smuggling in induction by treating corroboration as a report of past performance rather than a predictor of future success, though accepting this costs us any guarantee that the preferred theory will not fail tomorrow.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If corroboration is interpreted as increasing the logical probability of a theory, the defense collapses into the induction Popper rejected.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference implies an expectation that the theory will continue to succeed in the future based solely on past success, it commits the inductive fallacy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent cannot distinguish between acting on a convention and acting on a reasoned critical preference, the distinction between dogmatism and critical rationalism dissolves.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Preference via Severe Testing: The mechanism selects theories based on the severity and number of tests they have survived, interpreting 'preference' as a rational decision to act on the theory that currently possesses the highest informational content and has proven most resilient, without assigning it higher logical probability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
